Background · machine learning

Rules vs. learning

A normal program follows rules a human wrote: "if the pixel is dark, do X." But try writing rules to recognize a stop sign in an image — nobody can.

Machine learning flips it: you show the computer many labeled examples — images with the correct answer attached — and it learns the rules itself. That process is called training.

Output  a confidence per class — "sign: 92% · wall: 5% · floor: 3%".

Classic programming

Rules + data → answers

A human writes every rule. Breaks down on messy, real-world images.

Machine learning

Data + answers → rules

The computer finds the rules. You control it with examples and parameters.

Background · the model

What a CNN does

A Convolutional Neural Network is the standard network for images — a stack of small feature detectors:

  • Early layers detect simple patterns — edges, blobs
  • Later layers combine them — shapes, objects
  • Final layer gives each class a confidence score

Our model has two convolution layers plus one dense layer — small enough to run in real time on a microcontroller.

Our network, in short

input image 96×96 grayscale ↓ Conv1 — 8 filters // edges & blobs ↓ Conv2 — 16 filters // shapes ↓ Dense — 32 units // decisions ↓ confidence per class // sign / wall / floor…

Every number here is a hyperparameter you can tune.

Background · the runtime

TensorFlow Lite Micro

TensorFlow Lite Micro (now "LiteRT for Microcontrollers") is Google's ML runtime built for chips with only kilobytes of memory:

  • Core runtime fits in 16 KB of memory
  • No operating system, no standard libraries, no dynamic memory
  • Models are quantized to int8 — 1 byte per number instead of 4

Running AI directly on the chip is edge AI: fast, offline, private.

Why quantize?

Smaller & faster

int8 makes the model ~4× smaller and the math ~4× faster — the price is a tiny drop in precision, which rarely matters.

Why on the edge?

No server needed

No uploading images, no network delay — the camera and the decision live on the same chip.

Background · the hardware

The ESP32-P4

A high-performance SoC from Espressif, built for exactly this job — the big sibling of the ESP32-S3 you used in earlier labs:

Dual-core processor Camera support (IMX219) Rich peripherals Arduino IDE

It captures images from the camera module, processes them on-device, and runs TensorFlow Lite models in real time.

And the tool for today

TFLiteTraining app

A desktop app inspired by Google's Teachable Machine: collect samples, train a CNN, and export a deployable int8 model — without writing training code.

Workflow: Collect → Preprocess → Train → Preview → Export → Deploy

01

Task 1 · Toolchain and first flash

Setting up the ESP32-P4

Arduino IDE 2.3.10+ esp32 boards 3.3.1 esp32_mannual

Install the board support, flash the camera-streaming sample, and prove the port works.

Task 1 · Steps 1–4

Install the board support

  • Install Arduino IDE 2.3.10+ (arduino.cc/en/software)
  • Settings → paste the URL into Additional Boards Manager URLs
  • Board Manager → install esp32 by Espressif, version 3.3.1 exactly
  • Unzip esp32_mannual into Documents/Arduino/hardware/
https://dl.espressif.com/dl/package_esp32_index.json

Task 1 · Steps 5–8

Board settings and first flash

  • Tools → Board → ESP32_mannual → ESP32P4 Dev Module, copy the settings one by one (not Port yet)
  • Then select the Port your board is on
  • Upload the sample code — it streams grayscale images over serial
  • Serial Monitor shows garbled characters = the image stream = success!
  • Then close the Serial Monitor — it occupies the port the app will need

Checkpoint 01 · Setup

Show the camera stream.

Deliverable A

Sample code flashed

Upload succeeded with the ESP32P4 Dev Module settings.

Deliverable B

Stream seen — then closed

Garbled data visible in the Serial Monitor, and the monitor closed afterwards to free the port.

If no port appears — recheck the esp32_mannual folder path and the board settings table

02

Task 2 · The TFLiteTraining app

From samples to a trained model

Collect Preprocess Train Preview Export

Open template.tmproj and learn the three areas of the workspace.

Task 2 · The workspace

Three areas, one workflow

Sample Area

Collect & preprocess

Capture images from webcam, files, or the ESP32-P4 camera; clean them up for training.

Train Area

Train the model

Set hyperparameters and click "Train Embedded Model".

Preview Area

Test it live

Feed live camera images to the model and read its confidence.

Task 2 · Sample Area

Collecting samples

Three sources — use Device to capture straight from the car's camera:

  • Webcam — laptop camera (pick it via the Gear icon)
  • Upload — picture files from your computer
  • Device — the ESP32-P4 serial camera

Device defaults: 96×96 · grayscale · 115200 baud · sync header AA 55 AA — they match the flashed code; don't change them.

Make one class per category, and keep the sample counts roughly equal (30–50 each).

Task 2 · Preprocessing

Cleaning the data

  • ROI — the purple box: only this region is kept
  • Dark Thr — darker-than-this pixels → white
  • Lum Thr — brighter-than-this pixels → white
  • Auto mode — crops the darkest area for you; Manual ROI — you drag the box

Remember  press S to save after any change — and processed images are resized to image-size² for training.

Task 2 · Train Area

Hyperparameters — the knobs of training

ParameterDefaultWhat it changes
Image size96Input detail vs. speed (96 / 160 / 384)
Batch size16Samples per step; more = faster, more RAM
Epochs20Passes over the data; too many → overfitting
Validation split0.25Fraction held out to check the model
Learning rate0.001Step size; higher = faster but unstable
Conv1 / Conv2 filters8 / 16Feature detectors per layer
Dense units32Neurons in the decision layer

The trade-off  bigger models may score higher — but always run slower. Real edge AI is finding the balance.

Task 2 · Preview Area

Test it live, then export

  • Gear icon → source Device + the right port
  • Toggle Input — live camera view
  • Read the confidence bar (switch % / score)
  • ROI shows what the model sees; Orig shows the processed image
  • Happy with it? Export model → menu → Save Project

Diagnosis tip  high validation score but poor live performance = overfitting or too little variety in your samples.

Task 3 · Deploy

Run it on the chip

  • Copy these five files from the export folder into the TFLite.ino project:
tm_model_data.cpp // the quantized weights tm_model_data.h model_resolver.h model_settings.cpp model_settings.h
  • Check IMG_SIZE matches the app's image size (default 96) — a mismatch breaks inference
  • Upload TFLite.ino, open Serial Monitor — your model is classifying live

Checkpoint 02 · Wrap-up

Show live inference on the board.

Deliverable

Demo on the chip

The exported model classifying the live camera stream with sensible confidences.

You learned

Data quality matters

ROI and thresholds often improve results more than a bigger model.

You learned

Every knob is a trade-off

Size, speed, and accuracy pull against each other — that's edge-AI engineering.
